title: Todd Monken Press Conference from the 2026 Annual League Meetings
text: You you start on April 7th. Is that correct? Yep. What's the How do you create an off-season program as a head coach for the first time in the Well, you take from where you've been before. I think that's where you start with the off-season. And then we have we get an extra non-mandatory mini-camp, which will be the week of the draft. Which will be great to be able to get on the field with them. So, that'll be that'll be exciting for us to get started there, but it's really no different. We'll start on April 7th. And phase one just get a chance to talk football and get the guys acclimated to the conditioning process. Is that the first day quarterbacks see the playbook? It's the first day that we're able to work with them on the playbook. They have them in possession? They have the ability to look at what we've already have what we already have. That's my thoughts, yes. But we cannot coach them on it. What have been your like your conversations with the players been like that that you've been able to have in the last couple of months? What's been How would you How would How would you sort of characterize those those those conversations? With With the players, I mean, when you've been able to just interact with them when they're in the building or It's been fine. When they've come through the building or when we've got a chance to talk to them on the phone or by text message, it's been fine. Have you been able to talk to Miles? We've talked back and forth. He has not been in the building as far as I know, so I have not seen him. Well, I wouldn't say they're going to be evenly dispersed, but we'll definitely disperse them to give ourselves a chance to at least evaluate who we have on the roster, whoever that might be as we go through the off-season. I know you said ideally you would like to go into training camp like knowing who the starter is, but is that is that realistic especially given like Deshaun is a player who hasn't really played live game reps in you know, almost three years now? you'd love to be able to come out of the spring with a depth chart. That doesn't mean there's still not competition. But I do think you have to narrow the reps that you or at least balance up the reps of who you anticipate has come out of the spring certainly in a position to be a starter. How does a one quarterback take the lead prior to training camp? By their play every day. I think every player does that throughout the off-season. Not only do they learn the system, but obviously there's got to be some competition in terms of what you do for the betterment of eight weeks cuz two of the weeks you're not even on the field, but the other eight weeks, what you see on an everyday basis. Again, it's just a small sample size cuz we don't have the pads on. So, it's mostly a mental competition at that point. >> Some of it can be that way, but obviously when you get into OTAs or you get into mini-camp, there is competition that takes place within the rules. So, yeah, I think you'll have a better idea of each position what their play looks like and then you take that into training camp, which is the closest thing you'll have to playing the games. Todd, when you evaluate draft quarterbacks, do you like to work them out? Do you feel like you get enough I think working quarterbacks out is a piece of that. I wouldn't say that's the obviously the most important piece of any player is their film. What they do either in the NFL when you're looking at free agents or in the draft, what they've done at the college level. I think workouts can be deceiving. Good or bad. It's weighed. It's a factor. When you When you are evaluating quarterbacks, how much do you take into account how the other 10 guys in the huddle or the other guys they work with respond to them? That's a part of it. That's a big part of it. Players being able to have a belief in whoever that player is. That's a huge part of it. But ultimately, it's what they the players' belief also comes with how those players play on the field. Todd, how much with this specific draft class you recruited a lot of these guys while you were at Georgia, whether it was Tyree or Garrett or or Cade. How much does that benefit you in terms of pre-established relationships with some of these guys as you're evaluating them? Some, but that people change over three or four years. I really haven't looked at much film from the past of Deshaun. I know he's going to be part of the roster and I know he's played at an elite level in the past. And we're excited to get to work with him. I know he's excited about getting back here and getting to work. I remember when you arrived in Baltimore, you spoke about wanting to really empower our backs in the line of scrimmage and really give them that full autonomy. As you start to evaluate these quarterbacks, are you approaching it with the same mindset that you want to give them full autonomy at the line of scrimmage? Does that Does that kind of play into the the quarterback competition decision? Sure. I think the the more you empower any player any person gives you the I mean, the optimal opportunity to get the most out of them. The more you empower somebody. Now, that just happens to be the quarterback position. What's been your first impressions of Shedeur and how do you evaluate him in the quarterback competition? Well, it's too early to really evaluate him other than it's been great that he's been in the building. It's It's refreshing to see a player that recognizes where he's at and where he wants to get to. And Gabriel hasn't been in the building? As far as I know, he has not. I have not seen him in the building yet. Deshaun was in early when I got the job, so I got a chance to sit down with him. It went great. No, he seemed excited and ready to go. Again, time will tell. Have you figured out what that horse's head gift was all about? It was my birthday. No, I mean, there was more than that. It was just happened to be my birthday. I haven't really drilled down yet exactly What was the relevance in him choosing a horse? He said he really liked it. Did he get one for himself? He said he was going to, but he he hasn't yet. What is it Is it ceramic or glass or what? I think it's I don't even know what porcelain is, but it felt porcelain. It was a clay or somewhat heavy. But it's a horse. Where is it? But it's It's right in between the Browns helmets right behind my desk. Yep. I just left it there. He's been in so often. You know, you change out pictures of people that come to the house. Cousins, aunts, uncles, relatives to make it whoever shows up. He comes in the most often, so I have his horse in it. If Deshaun gave me a an elephant, then I'd have the elephant up there as well. Todd, um given like the different stops you've had in college and and the NFL, what's maybe like your philosophy on on building out the wide receiver room in terms of skill sets and what you're looking for in in that room? I mean, it's real simple. Big, fast, physical, ball skills, run after catch. I mean, of course, that's what everybody's looking for. But I do think like any position, you're looking for a player that what is their elite trait? How can you continue to develop and round out the rest of their game? And how does it fit into what you want to do offensively? Todd, when you look at this specifically this tackle group and and I and you sort of peruse it. Do you see a relative lack of guys that are true left tackles in it compared to maybe some other cuz it seems like a lot of the top guys are right tackles who they're talking about flipping to the other side. Do you believe that to be the case? Um haven't drilled down that far into position specific. We've looked at all of the players. Have a pretty good idea of where we have them stacked. Andrew will have to speak more on that, but I think there's excellent depth in the old line room. And in some ways left tackle and right tackle sure, it's important the left tackle with a right-handed quarterback, but I know this, when T.J. Watt lines up on the right side, you'd feel a lot better if you had a really good right tackle. I mean, if my when my we were playing Miles and he jumps over there, we're not going to jump we weren't going to jump Ronnie Stanley over there, so you really need two tackles. Um certainly the left side is is critical. Where do you envision Hal Jenkins in the in the coming year on the line? Does he look like a center? Haven't gotten there yet. Certainly, we'd love for him to play guard. But he does give us the flexibility to play him at center depending on how the draft and our roster shakes out as we get closer to the season, but I love his flexibility. Give me that again. In the early part of the off-season conditioning Not at the facility. Not the first 2 weeks. Still can't throw at the facility. Well, shouldn't say that. First 2 weeks they can, we just can't be on the field with them. Then after that we'll be on the field with them. You'll gauge a little bit of where they're at from a physical standpoint and a mental standpoint, but until you actually get into phase three or the the the actually the other mini camp we have that's not mandatory, you really don't understand yet or you're not getting to uh really drilling down into where they're at. And then the final piece then training camp in the preseason. So that mini camp the week of the draft Yes, sir. It's 3 days, yes. Just like a mandatory mini camp it is time it is voluntary. But you could the time is the exact same. They can be there for 10 hours up to 10 hours a day, 24 hours over 3 days. You can practice. You just don't have a The difference is normally when you run your your other mini camp you have all the rookies. You have the players that have to be there. So we're probably looking at anywhere from 45 to 50 players. So rep wise you certainly can't can't rep like you would in a mandatory mini camp. You could rep 7 on 7? Everything. Everything you can rep just like an OTA practice. In that first time when you get them and you can do football stuff, how do you How do you divide the reps for the quarterbacks? Will they be divided evenly? Do you shift or I don't anticipate them being divided evenly. Even at the very beginning? I don't see it that way. I would just say it's our job to make any player feel comfortable wherever we put them. Certainly a player is going to be feel more comfortable where they played the majority of their snaps either at the collegiate level or the NFL level, but certainly it's our job to I mean I just read the other day that Sewell's going to move be moved to left tackle. Well, if you're a great player, you ought to be able to play left or right tackle, right? Don't don't restrict yourself to what I can and can't do. I don't I would never want to say that about a coach or a player. So you said that the reps aren't going to be divided evenly. So I assume like somebody's going to get more reps. Without, you know, looking at Deshaun's prior film or knowing how they fit in your offense, how do you decide who is kind of QB1 in terms of to start the offense or not? By basically what we've seen in the past and where the year ended last year. So is that each of them against the board for the reps or is I'm not ready to say that yet. I just said the reps The reps can't be divided up evenly. There's no chance of them being divided up evenly. At least on a daily basis. It's not ideal. I was at Georgia I think we had a four or five-way competition my first year there, the COVID year, and that was not ideal. Oh, great question. Um Well, working for Kirby Smart. Let's just put it that way. One of the elite coaches at any level. His work ethic, what he demands from players, I think it's hard to to not benefit from. Just like being with John Harbaugh. The last 6 years being with those two coaches, I think really gives you a pathway into um confronting anything that gets in the way of winning football. Todd, Dawand Jones and the center Luke Wypler, will they be ready for OTAs? Don't know that. I'm hopeful that by the end of OTA by the end of offseason we'll have them, but I don't know that for sure yet. Why do you think the league keeps skewing toward young offensive minds and why won't they give older guys a chance? I mean you and McCarthy get a third time around, but it just it doesn't seem to normally go that way. Why do you think that is? Oh, I don't I don't know. I don't I don't know exactly why other than I think there's a lot of really good coaches out there. I think the league is trending towards head coaches. I know it's trending towards head coaches calling their own plays. So I would also say that a lot of the non-play calling OCs or defensive coordinators are going to be young coaches. That's the way it's going to play out. It used to be there was probably about half of the head coaches in the NFL called their called offense or defensive plays, and now you're looking at almost 80% I think I counted up. So I think there's fewer and fewer older coordinators. I think that's part of it. Were you starting to run out of patience at all? Were you starting to run out of patience and wondering if this was ever going to happen? No. No. Wasn't meant to be. It's not meant to be. I mean, being an offensive coordinator in the NFL is pretty damn cool. I mean, if that would have been the end of it, then awesome. I mean, that's you're still one of the top 32 in the world at what you do, and I can't make decisions for people. You can only do the job that you have, try to do it the best of your ability, and if it works out, it works out. Coming into the organization here in your first year with a quarterback battle, can you speak to how you approach that from a leadership perspective, like being new to the organization, how you manage that? Can you speak if there's any advantage necessarily of being, you know, fresh to, you know, these players and being a head coach in that regard? Well, sure. The quarterback leadership's critical, but that happens organically. I don't think you can force somebody to be a leader that's not. I think you can talk to them about how they carry themselves, how their practice habits, their routine. But I think builds confidence with your other players players around them. Um I can't speak to being new and what that's going to do. we'll let let it play out. Right up in your first year here, will Switzer come back to the offensive meetings or will you? I'll run the offensive meetings. Most of them. I shouldn't say all of them. There'll be meetings that Travis will end up running, but for the most part I'll run the meetings, but we run them together. The installs are run together. Every coach has a piece of that. Most of the coaches will have a piece of the meetings, but for the most part I'll run the offensive meetings. And that's to install things the way you want. Correct. Do you have a fullback? We'd like to have a fullback. Why? Why is that? What do you What do you think that is? I think it's helpful in all the areas where you have to run the football. Coming out, 4-minute, short yardage, goal line. Especially if you want to be a gap scheme team. Don't think if you want to be a zone team per se you'd have to have that. But from gap schemes, downhill runs, and I think in those areas when you're trying to, you know, run the football to a high level, make them fit gaps, I think there's a benefit to having that. And we proved that with Evan Pryor Carter. So would you ideally like to have someone like in the same mold as Evan Pryor Carter or you open to maybe like a lighter body like a Kyle Juszczyk type or H-back type or Well, Pat's a unicorn. I mean, 300 lbs and basically with his athleticism, having an offensive guard back there with the field that he has, I think I think it's just it's rare. So we're going to look for any player that we think gives us an opportunity to run the football to a high level. No, I'm excited about the room. I'm excited about Shedeur, Deshaun, and Dylan. I mean, we'll see how it plays out through the draft or through free agency of adding another piece to that room. Early on it was different because you're hiring. That That's probably the biggest piece of it is hiring a staff. Cuz you're a part of it in the past, and I you got to go all the way back to Southern Miss, but not to the extreme of the pieces we had to put together here. Obviously at two critical spots, special teams coordinator and the defensive coordinator position that I thought would fit well with the current staff. So that was that was as much as anything. Everything else is getting ready for the draft. It's football. It's getting to know players. None of that's different in my opinion. What's your philosophy going to be on playing time in preseason games? You only have three of them. Do you favor playing rather than sitting? I anticipate playing our guys. How much that'll be determined, but I do anticipate playing our guys. All three parts of all three games? I don't know if I'd say all three, but at some part of the preseason, I anticipate our guys playing. Offensively, there's going to be a pretty big learning curve. Might be some formational things that are similar, defensively, I would anticipate there's going to be more similarity than there will be offensively. You run a lot of tall personnel and tight ends. It seems like there's also quite a few different looks now than maybe before. What's what's the value that you see, especially in your offense, to have something like Well, we were lucky enough at the place I was before to have a good number of tight ends. That also puts you in a position to use that personnel group. I wouldn't say we're going to be a 12 personnel group of 21 and 11 until we get out there and see what we have. Till we get the draft completed, free agency completed, and see what we have. I think that's our job as coaches is to utilize the players that we have. And we we morphed a little bit last year with Isaiah Likely being hurt and Lamar being hurt to a little bit more 21 than we were even 12 the year before. So, we'll see how it goes. I do think that the bigger you are, the calmer the looks. That doesn't doesn't mean it's an end-all, but I think the more open you are, the variety increases of what you see defensively, and the more up to speed your quarterbacks have to be in terms of protections and checks. I know you have your approach to the draft, but in the back of your mind, you're sort of thinking about how you can maybe add to your offense with some of these guys. 100%. But, the way it plays out out also has a a big part in that because you could have a player targeted and 30 picks later, he he didn't make it. So, it's you can't say for sure till you get the roster, and then you go from there. Why why don't we see much of 21 anymore in the NFL? I just think it's a byproduct of starts in high school. I think everything trickles down from that. That's why you're seeing more athletic quarterbacks. I mean, there are still quarterbacks, but in high school, you're using more athletic quarterbacks. You're not seeing tight ends. Blocking tight ends, they're playing defensive end. You don't see fullbacks cuz they don't exist. So, they're not trained to play fullback. Just like Charlie Kolar this past year in free agency was one of one, a blocking tight end that could block the C-gap. In the draft, there are a few more this year than there has in the past. So, it's hard to find those guys, and in a world of winning quickly, how long do you have to develop a player that isn't comfortable in that role? That makes it very, very difficult. The other is is you get to the point that if you haven't seen them on tape, you get to the point, a lot like they've done in the past here, use an offensive lineman in the backfield. Um use an offensive lineman as a as a blocking tight end. That's where you've seen more more jumbo packages because you just don't have those players coming out in the draft anymore or even playing it in in high school. I mean, when it comes to two backs in the backfield, that's nothing radical. No, it's not. >> Running backs all over in high school. Why why don't NFL coaches use two backs and both and that as an option to run You talking about just any backs or fullbacks in general? Just just two backs. It's not that that's not good football. I just think that you're comfortable with what you've done. That doesn't mean that's right. It's not about being right, it's about getting it right. But, when you don't see it or you're not around it, I I don't know triple option So, we're not going to run triple option. I've been around pieces of two back, two skill backs. So, we utilize those pieces. Haven't committed to more of that moving forward. Not that that's not You see it all over the place where you can still use it as pieces. You just don't see it as a general rule. Todd, a lot of a lot has been made about your affinity for for quarterbacks with mobility. Um just it's kind of open-ended, but like how much is like quote unquote mobility going to play a deciding factor in who starts at quarterback? I think most coaches would have an affinity for quarterbacks that are mobile, but they're also they also have an that can complete passes and are really good on third down and two minute. And so, that's a big part of it as well. So, certainly with the league and the way it's gone and the multiple looks you get defensively and the elite rushers that you get, it's certainly beneficial to have a quarterback that can escape, especially considering the number one pass play you're going to have in the NFL is scramble drill. So, it certainly benefits you to have a mobile quarterback, but ultimately, that's just a piece of it. That's that's a big piece of it, but I it's also you're not seeing nearly as many statues of quarterback. They don't exist. Colleges don't have them. High schools don't have them. So, they they really don't exist. I mean, players that are now considered less mobile 15 years ago would have been considered mobile. They're just not now because it's completely flipped to where there's a a lot more elite mobility guys than there's ever been. I think Shador is mobile. He's just not like some of the others. Yeah, I wouldn't say that. No, it's the same offense. It's just a matter of whether you want to use that athleticism. Whether you're When you install uh say for instance, you're running draws. What does it really take to install QB draw? Draw is already in. If you're running split zone and you're blocking the end, what does it really take to avoid the end and block the alley? It's just another piece of your offense that allows for a mobile quarterback to get on the perimeter. There's other aspects of that when you have a player like Lamar that you can take advantage of and be a little bit more extreme um than you are with with other quarterbacks, but for the most part, it doesn't change. As you look at you know, coaching Lamar, you know, kind now skewed what you you know, when you look at a quarterback or do you do you sort of have to factor in look, I'm not looking at you know, Lamar with such a one such a unique that you you take that into account as you're evaluating other quarterbacks? I just take it whoever's in the room. I really don't overthink it that much. We didn't know Lamar when we got there or I didn't. And you evolve as you go. What we started off with Lamar when I first got there, in the end, wasn't drastically different, but it was different. I don't I don't know the quarterbacks we have now other than what I've seen, and we really didn't know Lamar, and that's your job as a coach to evolve and build a system that fits the quarterbacks you have. He's a little like Brock Bowers in the fact that his his body type is more of an H and F, run after catch more than length, more as a C-gap blocking Y. So, you love his athleticism. You like his ability to run after catch, his ball skills like Brock, very similar in that regard. Having coached in the college level and now in the NFL as well, do you sort of see that finding sort of that those guys ready Andrew would have a better idea of that than I would over the years. I would just say that I think offenses have changed, the way teams practiced have changed. You have more college teams that run no huddle. You have more offensive linemen that are in two-point stances all the time. I think when you watch players on tape, O-linemen in college, their practices and their games are about stamina. There's no time to huddle, get right back to the line of scrimmage. How you teach O-linemen to finish in college is difficult. Cuz how do you have time to finish when you're right back on the ball? So, there's certain aspects of the game that has changed that certainly I wouldn't say prohibits O-linemen from developing, that's unfair. Again, Andrew will be able to speak to I know the players are more talented than ever. Their size, their athleticism, um their understanding of the game to me are at an all-time high. Is there a type of receiver that you guys might think could complement what you guys already have? And what do you kind of make of this uh draft class? I don't think there's anyone in particular other than we're obviously looking to add talent. Todd, uh I think George Warhop was your first hire. Is He was one of our first hires. >> to that? Oh, without a doubt. I think hiring Travis Whitzell, George Warhop, Danny Briere, Ian Coley, Jeff Blasko, who was here with me in '19, and Mike Vrabel, I mean what an elite staff. And then to have been with those guys before and to allow you to get up to speed quickly, and George and I are aligned as Travis and all of us are in terms of who we want as our offensive line coach, and that is to be able to run off the football and make them deal with us. And that's an old-school mentality, and that's what we want. Todd, Todd, I'm going to ask you as part of your coaching journey, it began in Tampa for you as a play-caller at the NFL level. What was your your takeaway from your time with Dirk Koetter, Mike Evans, and Chris Godwin, and did it help get you here? Well, first of all, I owe a lot to Dirk. I mean, Coach Koetter's been probably my number one mentor in terms of game planning, in terms of detail, how you approach attacking a defense, being a professional film watcher. I mean, I wouldn't be where I'm at where where I'm at without Coach. But and I'm certainly appreciative in '18 he gave me the opportunity to call it, changed my path forever. But one thing Dirk's always been about is how are you going to be explosive? And you look at any of his offenses and what I learned there was after turnovers, you want to be really good on offense and you want to be really good on defense. Be explosive and stop explosives. And that's the nature of the game. And then there's others that fall in line, but and we had really good players. So, I've I certainly benefited by having those players uh there, uh James and Fitz and all those wide outs and the great O-line we had, um wouldn't be where I'm at without Coach. Well, I think there's always competition irrespective of the number of reps a player gets. The number of reps a player gets doesn't eliminate competition. It's just in a given day, let's say for instance, you want to see a quarterback with the first group, the second group, the third group. Well, are you going to divide those reps up evenly? Are you going to divide up the reps everywhere evenly? Um I don't see it that way. I don't see it That doesn't mean there's not competition. I just see it as in a given day, and it'll be daily in terms of who gets what reps and when. Cuz we certainly want to allocate our reps to the players we feel like are going to give us the best chance to win. So, let me make sure I have this right. on a Monday, maybe someone gets more reps than on Tuesday, so someone else starts. Could certainly be that way. It's not written It's not written in stone. It's not like you're going to have like a QB1 Mhm. On any given day, that's we're flexible in that. Just like the practice schedule itself is always flexible. You could ask me about a practice schedule and we could change that tomorrow. That's not written in stone. How players compete, how they approach their job and their everyday uh diligence, that's non-negotiable. But how we do things, the number of reps we get, that's an everyday decision. Todd, when you say that, you said that you you really haven't looked at prior Deshaun film. But why wouldn't you look at, you know, prior games that he played, even in Cleveland and like, you know, in the same way that you watched Shady and kind of I just haven't drilled down into Have I watched a little bit of it? Of course, that is. But there's also some aspects of it. Okay, so I would say this. We have crossover tape. Have I seen Deshaun Watson play before? Of course. I saw him play against us when I was in Baltimore. Do Did we play the Cowboys 2 years ago after Cleveland opened up the season with Dallas? Yes. Is that a great film to watch Deshaun Watson on? Absolutely not. I mean, that was not a fun tape to watch to try and look at that film and say, "That's Deshaun Watson." It's unfair. So, I think you want a little bit cuz I don't know the system they changed to. I'm making a point here. When Ken Dorsey came in and what they were running, I don't know that. I don't know what they were asking him to do. Or the year before when the Browns came over and beat the Ravens there. I don't know that. I just know what I've seen over the years. I've seen a really good football player. And we're hoping to be able to tap into that. I know he's excited and we're excited to work with him. Like we are with Dylan, uh like we are with Shady. I'll go back to Travis. When I first got to Baltimore, Greg Roman had been the offensive coordinator designing the whole run game. Where everywhere else I'd been, the O-line coach had a huge hand in the run game. So, when I got there, Joe D'Alessandris, who's passed away since then, he did more of the protections. When I interviewed Travis to decide whether just keep him on the staff, he went through the run game and absolutely killed it. And our job was to mix, blend what I've done in the past, and then what Lamar did well. And ever since then, he's just grown leaps and bounds in all aspects of his coaching. Not just run game, dealing with players, pass game, overall thoughts, philosophically how to attack people. Uh we wouldn't have had the success we had in Baltimore without him. All right, we got to wrap this up. Jimmy, uh you said yesterday Deshaun feels like he's getting a fresh start. Do you feel that way? In your conversations with him, do you kind of get the sense that he feels he's getting a fresh start? I think so. I spoke to him one day. I mean, I dated my wife for 5 years before we decided to get married, so one day is not enough. But I will say just like 2 weeks isn't enough, 2 months isn't enough. It's uh it's a process. I will just say this, we're excited to have him. We're excited to see what he has. He's part of our roster. Anybody that's part of our roster, it's our job as coaches to try and get the most out of them. Why isn't that obvious? I don't have any idea. I don't I don't understand it at all. The most important part is to put a winning product on the field. I don't care who that is, whether they're on our roster or they're not. Now, he just happens to be part of our roster. And I'm excited to have him along with the other players we have on our roster.

title: Brian Gutekunst 1-on-1: "We're excited to get going"
text: Hey everybody, Brian Gutekunst [music] joins us from the league meetings in Brian. For you, what's the most productive part? The formal meetings or the informal stuff with your colleagues from around the league? >> They're both important, but I think catching up with with you know, colleagues throughout the league is important and you know, and so that's but it's all important. You know, it's all all stuff that that we need to be aware of and you know, a lot of things that are talked about here, you know, they'll be continued conversations. Um it's been a good couple days so far. Draft coming up in about a month. Where are you at in that process? We're kind of in the middle of what we call phase three and we're in pretty good shape. [music] We feel really good about where we are with the board and our guys are just getting off the road a little bit now. There's a few pro days left that they're finishing up. Uh it'll be good next [music] week to get it back in the fold and and start going through the all the things that they've gathered over the last uh three, four weeks. At the combine, you said it's all about everything we do was about winning now. How good does this draft have to be to have an impact in that regard? title: Matt LaFleur 1-on-1: "We've got to figure out ways to finish games"
text: Hey everybody, head coach Matt LaFleur [music] joins us from the league meetings. And Matt, what's it like to have your brother Mike here as a fellow head coach? It's pretty surreal. [music] It's pretty It's a pretty cool experience. Um I'm looking forward to being around him and some of the other coaches and uh make sure we uh give him a hard time once we get all get together. Back home, a number of changes on your coaching staff. Jonathan Gannon, your new defensive coordinator. [music] When he was hired, there was a lot of talk. Is he a 4-3 guy? Is he a 3-4 guy? In today's game, Matt, does it really matter? Uh I don't think it does. I think it's about our players and trying to put them in the best position possible. I think, you know, Hafley was a four-down guy and we got to a bunch of 3-4 type principles in our base defense. I mean, the majority of the game nowadays is played with your nickel defense out there, which is primarily a four-man front. But, you know, then again, you can get into odd spacing and some of those 3-4 structures out of nickel defense. So, I think I would say it's fluid in [music] terms of, you know, how we're going to build this thing. Jordan Morgan, is he ready to take over at the hot corner full-time? Yeah, I think so. I think last year and everybody gets sick of me saying it, but we're trying to get the best five out there and we thought for our team, it was best with to go with Sheed and putting him at guard. But, it wasn't necessarily as they were competing [music] for that spot, we would have been perfectly comfortable with Jordan at left tackle. It's just trying to find the best five that fit together. Your past couple months, you've had a chance to go through the cut-ups, look back at last season. What are you [music] taking away? What are you gleaning from that? Well, I think there was a lot of opportunity there that we didn't capitalize on and I think that's got to be the mindset coming in as we got to figure out ways to finish games and just be productive in those critical moments. I think when you look at it, it's kind of bizarre, but like three games where we don't punt on offense and we lose all three of those games. Like, that can't happen and we got to be better and it starts with us as coaches and then ultimately our players got to go out there and execute. Couple of those players, Micah Parsons, Tucker Kraft, big-time guys. How are they progressing health-wise? They're doing a great job. I think they're they're both putting in the work. They've attacked this thing with the right mindset. I think our trainers have done a hell of a job with them. That'll be a huge boost for our football team when we get those guys back and they're healthy and ready to go. Matt, have a good couple days. Thank you. Thanks, Larry.

title: One-on-one with Colts Owner & CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon | The Colts Show | NFL | Podcast
text: All right, well, and that's a lot of the guys that they're like, "You're going viral." I was like, "What does that mean?" You were going viral for things you've been doing for years. text: How many of these head coaches do you actually know? >> That's a No, that's a great question. I never thought about it. Probably more than I thought I've worked with. So, I feel like I know a lot of them. >> Um, I want Malik to be himself. Um, there's there's nothing I'm going to sit here and say that I want this, this, this, and this. I think he's got great leadership qualities that guys will rally around. I've seen it. Um these guys have seen it. Um and I've seen what we can do on the field. He needs to develop. He needs to continue to grow. But I'm not going to I'm not going to put any expectation on what I want to see from him. Why do I like him as a person? I mean, just you guys, when you start to be around him, you'll see it. He's humble. He's um got this way about him where he connects with his teammates. It's the way he treats people. It's the way he works, which to me is probably more important than anything. I just I think the more you guys are around him and the more he's around his teammates, everybody will start to see it. Um, and I'm going to be excited for you guys all to experience that. The type of person that he is, the type of worker that he is, the way he'll treat the media, the way he'll treat his teammates, and the way he'll be with his coaches and his teammates. There's There's three things when I watch a corner's tape, when I evaluate a tape that I always look at. There's three levels of play that I want to see if they can win at. One is the line of scrimmage. I call that level one. Can he win at the line? Can he press? Can he make a guy stop and start his feet? Can he use his hands? Is he quick enough to change direction? Right? Can he take good cut off angles? When a guy steps out and goes in, is he fast enough to come back inside? So, can he win there? Level two is all the intermediate routes, right? All the inb breaks, the digs, the comebacks. Can he drop his hips and accelerate out of his cuts? Or is he a high hip guy that can't do that? And maybe he doesn't have to do that because he can win so well to line of scrimmage. And then level three is can he win down the field? Can he make a play down the field? Now, I don't know if you're going to find many that can be elite level one, level two, level three. Those are the Derell Rivases of the world and the Hall of Famers, right? Um, and I've been fortunate enough to see some of those guys and coach some of those guys. But then you look to see, can they at least do two out of the three? And then you're then I go from there and then it's can they do one out of the three. If if they can't do any out of three, then we're probably going to have to find a different player. I want guys who can kind of as I call the game through those guys can kind of react and communicate with me and tell me what they see and I can kind of play with the game within the game with the opposing quarterbacks with those guys. The ball can't get behind you. And then the skill sets after that is there's some that are really good in man coverage, some have really good range. Um, some are really physical, some have all of it. title: Mark Wilf Talks Offseason, Quarterback Room, Rob Brzezinski, 2026 NFL Draft & General Manager Search
text: Here out at NFL owners' meetings, we are joined by our owner, Mark Wilf. How are you doing today? Doing great. Thank you. Okay, well, we got to get into the into the big questions. I know you have spoken at length about your confidence in Rob Brzezinski and what he brings to the table in this interim role right now. How did you evaluate what he was able to do in a challenging off-season? Well, I think I think between him and Coach O'Connell, they've done a great job putting our football coaching staff, personnel staff together and really going about the decision-making in an intentional way, strategic way, transparent, a lot of communication going on. So, good decisions so far. Right. I know you have a great relationship with him. What is something that he's done that may have impressed you while he's taken on more of a leadership role? >> I just think the way he's bringing people together and kind of getting everyone's buy-in in terms of every decision, including ownership, and really being thoughtful and intentional and patient in terms of making the moves at the right time. And also, some of the cap moves have been great. So, I think we've cleaned up some of the challenges we had there and we're ready to go for the draft. >> I bet. Well, before we get to that, there were several moves made, most notably Kyler Murray, a former first-round [music] draft pick. What excites you about adding more competitive depth there in the quarterback room? I think it's super important. Obviously, quarterback, the most important position in the in the field and [music] having a great quarterback room, J.J. McCarthy, Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz coming back after playing so well before his injury last year and Max Brosmer. So, we have a lot of great talent there, good blend of all kinds of experience and all kinds of talent. So, it's it's going to be great. You mentioned the draft and soon after that, you have also said that you'll start the the new general manager search. How does that process begin? How do you see it playing out? >> already laying the groundwork. Again, this is an ownership decision, very important for the club. But right, you know, we're really focused on the NFL draft. We've got nine picks. We're really excited about it. I think our fans should be as well. We're excited about that and focused on that. And then right after the draft, we'll get going in terms of interviews, getting the best candidates, talking through it and making sure we have the right leader for our organization. Well, we mentioned the draft and recently the Vikings have announced that [music] they're teaming up or partnering with the Minnesota Sports and Events, as well as US Bank Stadium, to put in a 2028 NFL draft bid. So exciting. How can that What kind of an impact does that have on the organization, on and off the field? Well, we saw in Super Bowl 52 and Minnesota knows how to put out big events. US Bank Stadium, the premier stadium in the world. So, we have all the attributes. We have a great business community, a lot of support. We have the CEOs of US Bank, Ecolab and Medtronic along with us leading this effort and I think we've got a great bit put together and hopefully the NFL will agree with us and get get us to the 2028 draft, but a lot of work ahead of us. On a personal note, as an owner, what [music] would it mean to you to be able to bring that to the Twin Cities? Very exciting. I mean, the community's been so good to us as ownership, to the Minnesota Vikings. We have great fans and I think the fans deserve an NFL draft. The community deserves it and we're going to work on getting it to to Minnesota in 2020. >> Yeah, fingers crossed on that one. One more thing before I let you go and enjoy the beautiful weather here in Phoenix. Girls flag football initiative has more than doubled here in Minnesota as far as the teams in the state. What about that excitement, that exuberance for participation impresses you the most? Well, I just think the [music] the empowerment girls flag football has brought, the incredible explosive growth all over the world, really, and the confidence that it it gives young women and and just the growth in Minnesota now in over 100 schools, 19 of the top 20 cities in Minnesota have flag football. So, hopefully Minnesota will join the 18 states that have already sanctioned it as a full high school sport and we think that's the sky's the limit as far as getting engagement in football. I hope so. Really wish that was around when I was a kid. Thank you, Mark. Appreciate your time. Thanks so much.

title: Former NFL GM Ran Carthon on Building a Roster | Giants Huddle | New York Giants
text: Welcome to another edition of the Giants Total Access brought to you by Citizens, the official bank of the Giants. I am John Schmelk. Very excited to welcome back to the show for a second time. He joined us back, I think, early September, late August to preview the season. We said we'd join up again before the draft, and here he is, former NFL general manager Ran Carthon. Ran, it's good to talk to you, man. How are you? Man, I'm good, man. Like we were just talking about off air, feeling old. Um went out of town one day this week, came back with a cold. Weak immune system. It's just life is life-ing. >> [laughter] >> Dude, I've been dealing with like hip bursitis for like 6 weeks, and I haven't been able to play basketball. It's been absolutely killing me, but it's just old man problems. That's pretty much what it is. Yeah, absolutely, 100%. But hey, I wouldn't have it any other way. Glad I'm above ground having these problems than than than the other side of it. Yeah, you're absolutely right. And look, this is the fun type of year, right? For for people like you, this is where you guys, you know, run your craft, make your money. So, you have the Giants here, you kind of go through free agency. I'm going to start big picture first, right? You go through free agency, you try to fill as many holes as you can so you're not trapped in terms of what you want to do in the draft. But a lot of these Giants signings, at least some of them, were one-year deals, like uh Greg Newsome corner, Dono Mooney, Calvin Austin at wide receiver. Um they haven't gotten a guy that you would think is going to be their starting right guard yet. When you think about guys on one-year deals, and then you start thinking about the draft, do they even kind of enter your thought process, Ran, in terms of when you assess your needs, or is drafting a guy such a long-term proposition, you almost act like those one-year guys almost aren't even here? You know what I mean? Yeah, no, the one-year guys are, you know, in most cases, uh they're bridges, right? Because you can't just assume, well, we'll get this guy in the draft, right? You don't know how the draft is going to fall, you don't know what moves are going to be made around you that will prevent you from getting a guy you covet. You don't I mean, obviously, the folks within the Giants front office, uh they're doing their homework, they have their sources, they have their resources to find out information, but you can't lean on that. And so, when an opportunity presents itself for you to be able to get a bridge, specifically a player you know or you've coached or coached against that you think can help you, um and help establish a new way cuz it's it's different from being a program where the head coach has been around a long time versus a new head coach coming in um that wants to implement implement his way of doing things, and you need purveyors of your message. You need guys that can carry your message throughout the locker room and be the epitome of what you want the Giants program to be moving forward. So, those one-year deals just kind of help you bridge the gap just in case, you know, you're not able to address those positions via the draft. >> I think that makes sense. When you look when you assess your needs as a general manager when you go into a draft, Ran, how much do you look 2 years down the road? This is a thing I did on our Big Blue Kickoff Live show last week and say, all right, well, I'm going to have a hole at this position in 2027 and this spot and this spot, I'm worried about that. Just an example, the Giants right now have don't have a guard or a center under contract for the 2027 season. I might think that's a problem. How much are you looking 2 years down the road and not just at this year when you're thinking about who you're going to draft? Yeah, I always say you got to have one foot in the current year and and one and your eyes out in the in the coming years, right? Because it's all it's forecasting. You got to see the future to a degree or understand what's coming in the future. How hard is it going to be to re-sign Kayvon Thibodeaux after this year with the amount of money that that position is getting and whether you feel like him or any other pass rusher is worth the money they're getting. That's the market. It's like the housing market, you know, you may not want to pay those prices for a home in a specific neighborhood, but if you want to live in that neighborhood, that's the price you're going to have to pay. And so, for the Giants, right, especially at the edge rush position, those are what I call first world problems. You know, you have three legitimate guys, three guys that we know can play in the league, that can get after the quarterback. And so, now you put yourself in a position where if you don't want to pay Thibodeaux after a couple years, and you know you have Abdul Carter. And someone that you believe that can be a solid replacement for Thibodeaux or or Brian Burns, for that matter. However they decide to do it within their organization. But, you know, to answer your question, you have you have to have, you know, your foot in 2026 and this cycle of player acquisition, but with your eyes to 27 and 28. Now, the other thing too, Ran, is that free agency is not over, right? The first wave is over, you could argue the second wave is over, but there's still a bunch of guys, mostly veterans, that are still out there. You know, maybe these guys are waiting for more money to come your way. Maybe these guys just don't want to do the off-season program, and they're happy to, you know, sign in July and show up for training camp. Um how much do you consider the conversations you might have had as a general manager with some of the free agents that are still available. And I'm thinking, let's say for say example, Greg Van Roten for the Giants. He was a starter the last 2 years at right guard, he's still a free agent. He signed late in the process his first year here. When you're thinking about what you have to do in the draft based on needs, and maybe what free agents you think you can still get in the building even after the draft? You get to May, June, and July, things like that. Yeah, I mean, you're looking at that. You're still monitoring, you're having, you know, whether if you're the Giants, whether it's, you know, Brandon Brown or Dennis Hickey or whomever, Tim McDonal, those guys are still staying in touch with these agents of the free agents that are out there. They're kind of keeping their eyes and their ears to the street, understanding what the market is, how much of the money is drying up because it's if you're if you're a free agent and you're still on the street because you're holding out with the hopes of having more money, you're just a bad business person, right? [laughter] Because the money's the money's drying up, and then now teams are going to have to I mean, it's already budgeted for, but you got to budget for your draft picks, right? And who who knows what may happen on draft night. You may acquire more picks, which now, you know, adds to that budget that you've allocated for being able to sign the draft picks. And you got to have operating expenses heading into the season. And so, that money is drying up. But I think, you know, for let's use the example you said Greg Van Roten. I'm sure they've been talking to his, you know, his people. And again, new regime. So, you know, the Greg Van Roten fit may not at necessarily fit, but I'm sure it does. And so, the conversation is probably being had with his team just in terms of, hey, we're still interested, what do you guys have? You know, if he wants to take his time, you know, there may be some other things that we're not, you know, privy to that may be going on. But you're having those conversations, you're keeping your ears and your eyes open to it. I know for myself, um I think it was, yeah, my first year in the chair, um signed DeAndre Hopkins late in in the process. Um and I think but I think he got released. I think he had a post-June 1 designation. But it was all things that we had understood what were going on, still understanding there are some cap casualties who may be cut. Um just again, with the understanding of what's to come, that forecasting I was talking about previous. Yeah, exactly. And if not Van Roten, then, you know, Daniel Fallale was someone that was with Harbaugh. Kevin Zeitler was someone that was with Harbaugh, right? And one of those guys at guard that you think can kind of bring in and and play that spot if you don't end up drafting um one of those players. All right, let's talk about the draft process now. As a general manager, what did you get out of this part of the process, where you're going to pro days, you're seeing guys work out, you're doing the 30 visits? What are you trying to achieve in this, you know, last run-up of 3-4 weeks before the draft? Well, I'll be honest with you, I always call this is um I call the earlier part of process everyone being nosy, right? It's because everyone's trying to figure out what what the next person is doing, who likes who, who's showing up where. So, you know, for me, pro day, uh for some of the guys that I may not have been able to see move around live, I would like to see them move around live. Uh again, for me, it's I take a different approach to it, um cuz I lean heavily on the tape and what the tape has shown me over the last couple of seasons. But like certain positions, and I talked about this somewhere I was on air this week, um like the quarterback position. You know, I want to be at the pro day to see how his teammates respond to him. To see how people in the building react to him. See how he engages with people in the building. Um because to me, that tells you a lot about the person um and the human cuz I'm a big believer in that, being able to get the right type of person to come into and, you know, and insert them into not only the organization, but your city and your state um because they have to be good people. Um so, that that type of stuff is important, but then also, um again, and and and I have some of the stuff here in front of me just going back in my research cuz I was just recently at the University of Miami's pro day, where the Giants came out, um had a large contingency of people there. Those are some of the things I pay attention to, as well. I look at the trends. Like [snorts] um you know, for example, if back in the day with the Pittsburgh Steelers, if Mike Tomlin, Kevin Colbert, and uh I want to say Dan Rooney, if they were all at a pro day, you knew they were really interested in a particular player, right? And so, those are like the little things, those little type nuggets I'm looking at and trying to figure out, okay, I saw [snorts] Joe Schoen, I saw Brandon Brown, you know, I saw this person, I saw this person, I saw Dennis Hickey. I'm like, okay, who are they interested in? Right? And give that gives you tips because now if you're sitting there within that certain range, then you know, okay, and they've top-30 visited this guy, there's a chance that they're looking here, so we may and it's a need, so we may have to position ourselves to move ahead of them if there was a player that we specifically coveted. But just in terms of the evaluation process, I think I think I'd use the combine and the pro day more so to confirm what I've seen on tape. That makes sense. Um you know, if a guy goes out and he runs 4-3 then now I could go back to my notes and say, "Hey man, I thought this guy could really run on tape." So I'm I'm not wild and it it just because he runs 4-3 doesn't mean I'm moving him up four rounds, you know, on on my draft board just because he ran a specific time. I lean heavily on the tape and I judge more so the play speed than the necessary time speed. When you talk about play speed and you're right, you do watch that on tape. How much did you use and how useful did you find some of the college GPS data that that that you guys get now in terms of they give you actual play speed, some change of direction stuff sometime. How much did you use that and how useful was that in conjunction with the tape and some of the time stuff at the combine? No, you use it you know, obviously as a as a part of it. The greatest example I love to give is when I was in San Francisco and we were in the draft process and we were watching Dre Greenlaw, the linebacker. And I think at his pro day he may have ran like 4-7. And we were like "I don't know if that time is right. Like he he plays so much faster than 4-7." And so you know, we everyone was stumped, right? Everyone was stumped. And and it didn't help like Dre was 5'11, under 230 and then you run 4-7 you're like, "Ah, that's kind of a ugly card that you're looking at on the draft board." But then we was like, "Okay, well let's use our resources. Let's contact you know, our sources at University of Arkansas and let's let's get some of these GPS times." Well, you get the GPS times and you see that he's reached 20 miles an hour. He's reached 21 miles an hour. And this was back at a time where >> [snorts] >> the GPS times they just gave you that that one good burst. But now the GPS times can give you that max speed and how long they were able to hold that max speed, which I think is a is a better indication of how fast someone is versus that one quick burst. You don't know what that burst was. You don't know if he was in chase mode because he got beat, you know, >> and he's just just laying it all on the line and so you know, it's it's a better indication now of those you know, for the speeds, you know, because again you're watching play speed. You can understand better because I mean let's face it, some guys just can't run a 40. Right? And that's that's just is what it is or you have those guys that it's you don't have pads on and you've trained for it and you're just running in a straight line for 40 yards as fast as you can. Well, we all know and John, you've been around the game a ton of years. You know when you're playing on the actual football field, instincts have a part into it, right? So if you know you could be you could run 4-2, but if you don't know where you're going, you're not going to move as fast, right? So so all those things come into account. But to answer your larger question, you use the the GPS times to kind of again confirm what you've seen on tape. And also you can run really well when you're in shorts and a t-shirt. When you're worried about guys hitting you, you might not be running as fast on the field either, which is part of the scenario there as well. Joined by Ryan Carthona, he's the host with Ryan Wilson on the with the first pick podcast on CBS. We thank him for joining us. You mentioned traits when you talk about Dre Greenlaw. Did you have thresholds at each position? How hard and fast were you with those thresholds in terms of height, weight, length, stuff like that? I feel like this draft class there's a lot of outliers at a lot of different positions. Like so how did you treat those traits and kind of what you found were your thresholds at positions and and just kind of how you work through that part of it? Oh yeah, we definitely had again, we're we're in the data age now. And so you have all the historical data you know, based on your offensive, defensive, special team systems, you have specific size size, speed, length thresholds. One of the cool things that this whole Shanahan, McVay, LaFleur tree specifically with their offenses, they have well, we we would have meetings that we call profile meetings, profile tape meetings where every position coach would put together a profile of what they wanted their room to look like. So if you're a wide receiver coach, you're going to come in and you're going to have your your wide receiver profile tape meeting. You're going to have what you want your X to look like, what you want your Z to look like, what you want your F. And then they even went as far as giving us the prototype. Right? So at the prototype X, Julio Jones. Prototype Z is you know, Davante Adams. Prototype F, you know, let's say Wes Welker or whomever. Whatever it is that you're wanting out of those positions and then give us clips. You get clips of how you know, when we say, "Hey, double up at the line of scrimmage." Here's 10 clips of what we're talking about. You know, when we're talking about being able to stack you know, the corner at the line of scrimmage, here's what we're talking about. So you get those tapes and what that what that allows the it makes the scouts' job easier. Cuz now you can you can take the guesswork out of it. You know specifically what fits in your system. And the cool thing for you guys is you guys have a new defensive coordinator in Donard Wilson who I've worked with at two different stops. We worked together at the St. Louis / LA Rams and then we worked together most previously in Tennessee. He has that for his defense. Right? He knows exactly what he wants at every single position, what it looks like and can give you the example of what it looks like. So it's going to make the scouts' job easier to pull defensive players that fit Donard's system. Same thing with the new pass game coordinator and obviously worked with him here, Brian Callahan. Because of his previous experiences, he knows exactly what he wants in the quarterback. Now you guys are in a unique position cuz you already have a quarterback. Um but you know, moving forward, what does he want out of the backup quarterback? What is what are the traits that he's looking for in having the next guy behind Jackson Dart? So that's going to make the scouts' job easier. And again, you go back I mean, just take it all the way now to the top of John Harbaugh. When John Harbaugh took over as the head coach of the Baltimore Ravens the Raven way, if you will, had already been established. There are only certain teams in the league where it's the Baltimore Ravens, it's the Pittsburgh Steelers. When you say those two franchises' names an image of what that player looks like immediately comes to your head. Right? And that's what the Giants used to be back in the day when when it was a Parcells team, you knew exactly you know, what a New York Giant looked like. He was a literal giant. You know what I mean? And so I think you guys will get back to that way where there will be a certain fit type of certain fit and style of player that will symbolize what a New York Giant is. And that's what you that's what this defense will look like, a bunch of disciplined with grit. Obviously with with with Matt Nagy coming over as the offensive coordinator. >> Cuz you got Nagy, you got Roman, you got Callahan. All of them kind of three different systems, right?
